snippets.title: Combustion leak (block) test
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.

snippets.title: Misfire under load from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire under load may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.title: Misfire while idle from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire while idle may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

messages.content: Our family's 2017 compact crossover with the 2.4L and the automatic transmission, just past 160,506 miles. It bucks under load, like merging onto the highway, and the scan tool shows P0303. No problem at idle, rain or shine. Any idea which check to begin with?

snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

snippets.title: Overheating at idle from a restricted radiator core
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at idle and in traffic. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

messages.content: Shop ticket: 2014 hatchback, 1.6L, stick shift, odometer 67,696. Got stuck in a drive-through line and the temp gauge went almost to the red. Once I got back on the road it came down. It never runs hot at highway speed. One more thing: clunk from the front end, right side, on rough pavement. snippets.title: Warm AC at idle from an inoperative condenser fan
snippets.text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan, model years 2009-2021. Vent air may blow warm when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.

snippets.title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the steering wheel may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2015. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on hot restarts. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

Lean codes with high long-term fuel trim at idle may set when a contaminated sensor element under-reports airflow. With the engine warm and idling and all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement. Do not touch the sensor element. Repair: clean the sensor element or replace the sensor.

snippets.title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes and a manual-clutch transaxle. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.

snippets.title: Front clunk when turning slowly from worn strut upper mounts
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk only while you are turning slowly. With a helper bouncing the front, rest a hand on the upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop. Repair: replace the upper mounts and bearings.

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to midsize sedans, small crossovers and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the front seatback may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

snippets.title: Rotor thickness variation
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes, model years 2016-2021. Using an outside micrometer, measure rotor thickness at eight evenly spaced points about 0.5 in from the outer edge. Thickness variation must not exceed 0.0005 in. Variation above this limit produces pedal pulsation during braking from speed. Clean rust scale off the measuring track first.

snippets.title: Lower ball joint play check
snippets.text: Applies to midsize SUVs, minivans and compact crossovers. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

messages.content: I bought a used 2012 hatchback with the 1.6-liter four and manual; it shows 41k miles. Shimmy in the steering wheel only when braking from 60 mph or so. Light stops around town on smooth roads are fine. Can you point me to a good starting check?

snippets.title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes and an automatic transmission. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.

snippets.title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes and a manual-clutch transaxle. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.

snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

messages.content: The brake pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes when I brake from highway speed on dry pavement. It's smooth when I'm not braking. This is my 2019 small crossover. It has the 1.4L turbo, the CVT and about 109,943 miles. How would you approach this first?

snippets.title: Front clunk over bumps from worn strut upper mounts
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk over bumps or when turning slowly. With a helper bouncing the front, rest a hand on the upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop. Repair: replace the upper mounts and bearings.

snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side. Probe the terminals themselves, not the cable clamps, so a loose clamp shows up.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Coolant loss with no visible leak from an early-venting cap
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. Coolant may drop slowly with no visible leak when the pressure cap vents early and coolant escapes through the overflow as vapor. Fit the cap to a pressure tester adapter and pump until it vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. Repair: replace the pressure cap.

snippets.title: Dim lights at idle from a slipping accessory belt
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Lights may dim at idle under load when a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

snippets.title: Recharge check for repeat dead batteries
snippets.text: A battery that is not brought back to full charge during normal driving goes flat after several days parked even with no excess draw. After a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts. A reading of 13.5-14.7 V shows the charging system is recharging the battery. Measure at the posts, not the cable clamps.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, minivans and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2015. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. messages.content: Mine is a minivan from 2012, 3.5L V6 under the hood, auto trans, 125k miles so far. The brake pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes when I brake from highway speed on dry pavement. It's smooth when I'm not braking. Can you point me to a good starting check?

snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. snippets.title: Misfire under load from a tracked or fouled spark plug

messages.content: This is my 2016 minivan. It has the 3.5L V6, the automatic and about 35,202 miles. Misfire code P0304. I feel a stumble going up long grades or when passing, never at idle or cruising. Weather doesn't seem to matter. What should I test to start narrowing it down?

snippets.title: Lean code at idle from cracked PCV hose

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.

snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

snippets.text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan, model years 2009-2021. Air only warms at idle when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.

snippets.text: Applies to midsize SUVs, minivans and compact crossovers. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: On 2016-2021 models, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

messages.content: Hi. 2019 compact sedan, 2.0L four-cylinder engine, automatic, roughly 176k on the odometer. The battery light flickers at idle and the headlights dim, and they brighten when I rev the engine. It happens warm or cold. What's a sensible first test here?

With the engine off, inspect the accessory belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs and confirm the tensioner indicator is within its marked range [SM 6.2.8]. Write down the reading so we can compare it to spec.
Checked it. The belt looks new, no glazing, and the tensioner mark is in the middle of the range.
Normal there. With the engine at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, measure AC ripple voltage across the battery posts and compare it with 0.5 V AC [SM 7.8.1].
AC ripple measured well under half a volt. Can we stop testing? I'll grab a alternator on the way home.

The plug from that cylinder looks clean and is gapped right, no tracking on the porcelain. Still nothing obvious. Just tell me the spark plug is bad so I can move on.

snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: On 2016-2021 models, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side. Probe the terminals themselves, not the cable clamps, so a loose clamp shows up.

snippets.title: Dim lights at idle from a slipping accessory belt
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Lights may dim at idle under load when a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

snippets.title: Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2015. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.title: Front clunk over bumps from worn strut upper mounts
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk over bumps or when turning slowly. With a helper bouncing the front, rest a hand on the upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop. Repair: replace the upper mounts and bearings.

snippets.title: Automatic transmission fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: CVT fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2011-2021. snippets.title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the steering wheel may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on hot restarts. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

snippets.title: Long crank on cold starts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on cold starts. On any cold start, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Overheating in traffic from an inoperative electric radiator fan
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with electric radiator fans. Temperature may climb at idle and in traffic, but not at speed, if the fan does not run. With the engine warm and idling, turn the AC on or command the fan on with a scan tool. The fan should start within a few moments. Repair: repair the fan circuit or replace the fan motor.

snippets.title: Coolant loss with no visible leak from an early-venting cap
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. Coolant may drop slowly with no visible leak when the pressure cap vents early and coolant escapes through the overflow as vapor. Fit the cap to a pressure tester adapter and pump until it vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. Repair: replace the pressure cap.

snippets.title: Coolant loss with a dripping leak from an early-venting cap
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. snippets.title: AC operating pressure check
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines, model years 2010-2022. Connect a manifold gauge set to the service ports. With the engine at 1,500 rpm, the AC at maximum and doors open, compare readings with the chart for the ambient temperature. At about 80 deg F, typical readings are 25-45 psi on the low side and 150-250 psi on the high side. Wear eye protection at the ports.

snippets.title: Compressor clutch engagement check
snippets.text: Applies to models with a clutch-driven compressor, model years 2016-2021. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

snippets.title: AC operating pressure check
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines, model years 2010-2022. Connect a manifold gauge set to the service ports. snippets.title: Warm AC at idle from an inoperative condenser fan
snippets.text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan, model years 2009-2021. Vent air may blow warm when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that worsen as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

snippets.title: Dim lights at idle from a slipping accessory belt
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Lights may dim at idle under load when a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

snippets.title: Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

snippets.title: Charging voltage test under load
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2015. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights, blower on high and rear defrost on, measure voltage across the battery posts with a digital meter. Expect 13.5-14.7 V. A reading below 13.0 V with loads on indicates low charging output. Clean any corrosion from the posts first so it does not skew the reading.

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes and an automatic transmission. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines. snippets.title: Misfire while idle from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire while idle may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.title: Overheating in traffic from an inoperative electric radiator fan
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 3.4L V6 and 5.5L V8 engines with electric radiator fans. Temperature may climb at idle and in traffic, but not at speed, if the fan does not run. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test

With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

messages.content: This is my 2014 full-size pickup. It has the 5.5-liter V8, the automatic and about 141k miles. Got stuck in a drive-through line and the temp gauge went almost to the red. Once I got back on the road it came down. It never runs hot at highway speed. Any idea which check to begin with?

snippets.title: Spark output test with an adjustable spark tester
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with individual coil-on-plug ignition. Remove the coil from the misfiring cylinder, connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV between the coil and engine ground, and crank with fuel disabled. A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.

snippets.title: Engine and transmission mount check
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2016-2021. With the hood open, the brake held firmly and the engine idling, have a helper shift between drive and reverse while you watch the engine. Lift of more than about 0.5 in, or a visible gap at a mount, indicates a broken mount that can make normal shifts feel harsh.

snippets.title: Coolant level and trapped air check
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. With the engine cold, remove the radiator cap or degas bottle cap and check that coolant is at the neck or the cold-fill line. Never open the cap on a hot engine. Low coolant, or air trapped near the thermostat housing, causes temperature to swing upward at idle while airflow at speed can mask it.

snippets.title: Front clunk over bumps from worn strut upper mounts
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk over bumps or when turning slowly. With a helper bouncing the front, rest a hand on the upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop. Repair: replace the upper mounts and bearings.

snippets.title: Lower ball joint play check
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

snippets.title: Compressor clutch engagement check
snippets.text: Applies to models with a clutch-driven compressor, model years 2016-2021. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on hot restarts. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

A reading of 13.5-14.7 V shows the charging system is recharging the battery. Measure at the posts, not the cable clamps.

snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2015. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.

A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that worsen as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.title: Cranking compression test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. Disable fuel and ignition, remove all spark plugs and crank each cylinder through at least five compression strokes with the throttle held open. All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.

A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.

messages.content: Mine is a midsize sedan from 2017, 3.5-liter V6 under the hood, automatic transmission, 100k miles so far. Misfire code P0302. I feel a stumble going up long grades or when passing, never at idle or cruising. Weather doesn't seem to matter. Can you point me to a good starting check?

Good details, thanks. The first check is this: connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV to the coil from the misfiring cylinder and crank with fuel disabled, watching for a strong blue spark on every crank [SM-7118].
My buddy says skip the tests and get a fuel injector. Thoughts?

Ordering parts without a test risks money on the wrong one. Connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV to the coil from the misfiring cylinder and crank with fuel disabled, watching for a strong blue spark on every crank [SM-7118].
Okay, you talked me into it, and here's what I got. The spark tester showed a solid blue spark the whole time I cranked it.

Normal there. Pull the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a good cylinder, checking the gap and looking for a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or fouling [SM 1.9.8].

messages.content: I bought a used 2015 midsize sedan with the 3.5L V6 and auto trans; it shows 33k miles. It runs hot at idle. In stop-and-go traffic the gauge creeps up past the middle, but on the highway it stays right where it should. What's a sensible first test here?
With the engine cold, open the radiator or degas bottle cap and look at whether coolant is right up to the neck or the cold-fill line [B-24-067]. Let me know what you find.
Do I really have to test it? I'd rather just buy the thermostat.

Okay, you talked me into it, and here's what I got. Level is at the cold-fill line, nothing low.
That result clears it. With the engine warm and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool and confirm the fan starts [SM-2749].

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2010-2015. Lift of more than about 0.5 in, or a visible gap at a mount, indicates a broken mount that can make normal shifts feel harsh.

Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Cooling system pressure test
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines. With the engine cold, fit a cooling system pressure tester to the radiator neck or reservoir and pump to the pressure stamped on the cap. Pressure should hold for 15 minutes. While the system is pressurized, inspect the hoses, the heater hoses at the firewall, the water pump weep hole and the radiator end tanks for seepage.

snippets.title: Overheating at idle from a restricted radiator core
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at idle and in traffic. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

snippets.title: Cranking compression test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2016-2021. Disable fuel and ignition, remove all spark plugs and crank each cylinder through at least five compression strokes with the throttle held open. All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.

messages.content: It bucks under load, like merging onto the highway, and the scan tool shows P0301. No problem at idle, rain or shine. Our family's 2018 full-size pickup with the 5.5L V8 and the automatic, just past 99k miles. Any idea which check to begin with?

snippets.title: Dim lights at idle from a slipping accessory belt
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Lights may dim at idle under load when a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

snippets.title: Engine and transmission mount check
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2016-2021. With the hood open, the brake held firmly and the engine idling, have a helper shift between drive and reverse while you watch the engine. Lift of more than about 0.5 in, or a visible gap at a mount, indicates a broken mount that can make normal shifts feel harsh.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: Lower ball joint play check
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2016-2021. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.

snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: On 2016-2021 models, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side. Probe the terminals themselves, not the cable clamps, so a loose clamp shows up.

messages.content: Fleet unit: 2012 compact sedan, 1.8-liter engine, continuously variable transmission, 59k miles logged. Clunk from the front end, right side, on rough pavement. It definitely comes from the front, and it doesn't happen when turning sharply. What test makes sense right now?

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to midsize sedans, small crossovers and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.title: Charging voltage test under load
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights, blower on high and rear defrost on, measure voltage across the battery posts with a digital meter. Expect 13.5-14.7 V. A reading below 13.0 V with loads on indicates low charging output. Clean any corrosion from the posts first so it does not skew the reading.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that worsen as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that soften as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. snippets.title: Compressor clutch engagement check
snippets.text: Applies to models with a clutch-driven compressor, model years 2010-2015. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

snippets.title: Misfire under load from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire under load may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the front seatback may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

snippets.title: Spark output test with an adjustable spark tester
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with individual coil-on-plug ignition. Remove the coil from the misfiring cylinder, connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV between the coil and engine ground, and crank with fuel disabled. A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.

snippets.title: Lean codes at idle from a contaminated airflow sensor
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor, model years 2016-2021. With the engine warm and idling and all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement. Do not touch the sensor element. Repair: clean the sensor element or replace the sensor.

snippets.title: Warm AC at idle from an inoperative condenser fan
snippets.text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan, model years 2009-2021. Vent air may blow warm when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.

A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

At about 80 deg F, typical readings are 25-45 psi on the low side and 150-250 psi on the high side. Wear eye protection at the ports.

With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: CVT fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

messages.content: Shop ticket: 2010 minivan, 3.5-liter V6, automatic, odometer 33k. The automatic slams into second, a hard 1-2 shift, and it's worse once the transmission is fully warmed up. Any idea which check to begin with?

snippets.title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2015. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.

snippets.title: Lower ball joint play check
snippets.text: Applies to midsize SUVs, minivans and compact crossovers. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on hot restarts. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Long crank on cold starts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on cold starts. On any cold start, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

messages.content: Our family's 2014 hatchback with the 1.6L and the stick shift, just past 72k miles. When I stop for 15 to 30 minutes after driving, it cranks at normal speed for five or six seconds before it fires. Cold starts in the morning are instant. What should I test to start narrowing it down?

Good details, thanks. The first check is this: drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the fuel rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later; it should still be above 30 psi [SM 2.6.3].
Just finished that. Put a gauge on after a drive. Still 42 psi after twenty minutes.

Thanks for checking. With the engine fully warm, compare the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading at the thermostat housing; they should agree within 10 deg F [SB 19-335].
Coolant temp on the scanner and the IR reading were within a few degrees of each other. I've run out of patience with testing. Which part do I order?

snippets.title: Coolant level and trapped air check
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. With the engine cold, remove the radiator cap or degas bottle cap and check that coolant is at the neck or the cold-fill line. Never open the cap on a hot engine. Low coolant, or air trapped near the thermostat housing, causes temperature to swing upward at idle while airflow at speed can mask it.

snippets.title: AC warms only at idle from an inoperative condenser fan
snippets.text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan, model years 2009-2021. Air only warms at idle when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.

snippets.title: Overheating at speed from a restricted radiator core
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at speed and on grades. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

snippets.title: AC operating pressure check
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines, model years 2010-2022. Connect a manifold gauge set to the service ports. With the engine at 1,500 rpm, the AC at maximum and doors open, compare readings with the chart for the ambient temperature. At about 80 deg F, typical readings are 25-45 psi on the low side and 150-250 psi on the high side. Wear eye protection at the ports.

snippets.title: Compressor clutch engagement check
snippets.text: Applies to models with a clutch-driven compressor, model years 2010-2015. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

messages.content: Short version please, I only want to know what to buy. Mine is a hatchback from 2016, 1.6L four-cylinder under the hood, manual, 154,119 miles so far. The AC blows warm all the time from every front vent, driver and passenger side alike. It was cold last summer. The blower works on all speeds. snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.title: Engine and transmission mount check
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2016-2021. With the hood open, the brake held firmly and the engine idling, have a helper shift between drive and reverse while you watch the engine. Lift of more than about 0.5 in, or a visible gap at a mount, indicates a broken mount that can make normal shifts feel harsh.

messages.content: Fleet unit: 2016 full-size pickup, 5.5L V8, automatic, 50k miles logged. Hard, delayed shifts once the car is warm. The first few miles cold are actually smoother. Not sure if it's connected, but the battery keeps going flat over a long weekend. Once it's jumped it starts every day as long as I drive it daily. snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to midsize sedans, small crossovers and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.title: Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2016-2021. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Cranking compression test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. Disable fuel and ignition, remove all spark plugs and crank each cylinder through at least five compression strokes with the throttle held open. All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.

Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.title: Combustion leak (block) test
snippets.text: On 2016-2021 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.

snippets.title: Coolant loss with no visible leak from an early-venting cap
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. Coolant may drop slowly with no visible leak when the pressure cap vents early and coolant escapes through the overflow as vapor. Fit the cap to a pressure tester adapter and pump until it vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. Repair: replace the pressure cap.

snippets.title: Cooling system pressure test
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines. With the engine cold, fit a cooling system pressure tester to the radiator neck or reservoir and pump to the pressure stamped on the cap. Pressure should hold for 15 minutes. While the system is pressurized, inspect the hoses, the heater hoses at the firewall, the water pump weep hole and the radiator end tanks for seepage.

messages.content: Our family's 2020 midsize sedan with the 2.5L and the automatic, just past 172,648 miles. Coolant keeps disappearing, maybe half a liter every couple of weeks. No drips on the driveway, no steam, and the temp gauge stays normal. Can you point me to a good starting check?

With the engine cold, pressurize the cooling system to the cap rating and watch for a pressure drop over 15 minutes while you inspect the hoses, water pump weep hole and radiator tanks [B-18-084]. Write down the reading so we can compare it to spec.

Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

messages.content: This is my 2013 midsize sedan. It has the 2.5L four-cylinder, the automatic and about 119,871 miles. There's a clunk from the front left when I go over speed bumps or potholes at low speed, driving straight. Nothing when I turn the wheel in a parking lot. Can you point me to a good starting check?
With the vehicle on the ground, grasp each front stabilizer link and push and pull firmly while watching both ball studs for play [SEC 2.23]. Write down the reading so we can compare it to spec.
Checked it. Both stabilizer links feel solid with no knock.
Thanks for checking. With a jack under the lower control arm, lift the tire with a pry bar and watch the lower ball joint for any vertical play [TSB-0960].
No movement at the lower ball joints with the pry bar. Which test makes sense now that this one came back fine?

snippets.title: Cooling system pressure test
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines. With the engine cold, fit a cooling system pressure tester to the radiator neck or reservoir and pump to the pressure stamped on the cap. Pressure should hold for 15 minutes. While the system is pressurized, inspect the hoses, the heater hoses at the firewall, the water pump weep hole and the radiator end tanks for seepage.

snippets.title: Combustion leak (block) test
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.

snippets.title: Cooling system pressure test
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 5.5L V8 engines. With the engine cold, fit a cooling system pressure tester to the radiator neck or reservoir and pump to the pressure stamped on the cap. Pressure should hold for 15 minutes. While the system is pressurized, inspect the hoses, the heater hoses at the firewall, the water pump weep hole and the radiator end tanks for seepage.

snippets.title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the steering wheel may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on hot restarts. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. snippets.title: CVT fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: Automatic transmission fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: Rotor thickness variation
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes, model years 2010-2015. Using an outside micrometer, measure rotor thickness at eight evenly spaced points about 0.5 in from the outer edge. Thickness variation must not exceed 0.0005 in. Variation above this limit produces pedal pulsation during braking from speed. Clean rust scale off the measuring track first.

snippets.title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

snippets.title: Lean codes at idle from a contaminated airflow sensor
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor, model years 2016-2021. Lean codes with high long-term fuel trim at idle may set when a contaminated sensor element under-reports airflow. With the engine warm and idling and all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement. Do not touch the sensor element. Repair: clean the sensor element or replace the sensor.

messages.content: Got a 2011 minivan here, 3.5-liter V6, auto trans, around 60k miles on it. Pedal pulsation when slowing down from highway speed, felt mostly through the steering wheel rather than the seat. No vibration while cruising, and I'm not towing anything. I'd like to diagnose it properly. Where's a good starting point?

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, minivans and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.title: Cranking compression test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. Disable fuel and ignition, remove all spark plugs and crank each cylinder through at least five compression strokes with the throttle held open. All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.

messages.content: Shop ticket: 2016 minivan, 3.5-liter V6, automatic transmission, odometer 125,959. It bucks under load, like merging onto the highway, and the scan tool shows P0301. snippets.title: Front clunk over bumps from worn strut upper mounts
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk over bumps or when turning slowly. With a helper bouncing the front, rest a hand on the upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop. Repair: replace the upper mounts and bearings.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2016-2021. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.

snippets.title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes and an automatic transmission. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2016-2021. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: AC operating pressure check
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines, model years 2010-2022. Connect a manifold gauge set to the service ports. With the engine at 1,500 rpm, the AC at maximum and doors open, compare readings with the chart for the ambient temperature. At about 80 deg F, typical readings are 25-45 psi on the low side and 150-250 psi on the high side. Wear eye protection at the ports.

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that soften as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side. Probe the terminals themselves, not the cable clamps, so a loose clamp shows up.

snippets.title: Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2015. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.title: Misfire while idle from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire while idle may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2012-2020. P0171 (system too lean, bank 1) may set with a rough idle that is worst on a cold engine. With the engine idling, inspect the hose at the elbow and flex it gently while listening for a vacuum hiss. Repair: replace the PCV hose and clamp.

snippets.title: Overheating at speed from a restricted radiator core
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at speed and on grades. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

messages.content: Fleet unit: 2018 midsize sedan, 2.5L four-cylinder, auto trans, 49,891 miles logged. At stoplights at night the headlights and dash lights pulse dim and bright, and the battery warning light flickers, even on warm evenings. It's fine once I'm moving. How would you approach this first?

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that worsen as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2010-2015. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

messages.content: Our family's 2017 compact crossover with the 2.4L four-cylinder and the auto trans, just past 33k miles. Upshifts are harsh, especially 2-3, and there's a delay before it engages. It gets worse the longer I drive. One more thing: if the car sits for two or three days, the battery is dead. It starts fine with a jump and drives normally, and the weather has been mild. What's a sensible first test here?

snippets.title: Lean codes at idle from a contaminated airflow sensor
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor, model years 2010-2015. Lean codes with high long-term fuel trim at idle may set when a contaminated sensor element under-reports airflow. With the engine warm and idling and all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement. Do not touch the sensor element. Repair: clean the sensor element or replace the sensor.

snippets.title: Rotor thickness variation
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes, model years 2016-2021. Using an outside micrometer, measure rotor thickness at eight evenly spaced points about 0.5 in from the outer edge. Thickness variation must not exceed 0.0005 in. Variation above this limit produces pedal pulsation during braking from speed. Clean rust scale off the measuring track first.

messages.content: Hi. 2014 compact sedan, 1.8L four-cylinder engine, continuously variable transmission, roughly 78k on the odometer. Check engine light is on with P0171 (system too lean, bank 1). The idle is rough, worst for the first few minutes after a cold start. Can you point me to a good starting check?

snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

snippets.title: Lower ball joint play check
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

snippets.title: Front clunk over bumps from worn strut upper mounts
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk over bumps or when turning slowly. With a helper bouncing the front, rest a hand on the upper mount under the hood and feel for a knock. With the engine running, turn lock to lock and feel for binding or a pop. Repair: replace the upper mounts and bearings.

messages.content: Mine is a midsize sedan from 2015, 2.5-liter four under the hood, automatic transmission, 168k miles so far. Clunk from the front end, left side, on rough pavement. It definitely comes from the front, and it doesn't happen when turning sharply. What should I test to start narrowing it down?
With the vehicle on the ground, grasp each front stabilizer link and push and pull firmly while watching both ball studs for play [B-24-082]. Let me know what you find.
Do I really have to test it? I'd rather just buy the control arm.

Ordering parts without a test risks money on the wrong one. With the vehicle on the ground, grasp each front stabilizer link and push and pull firmly while watching both ball studs for play [B-24-082].
Went out and checked it like you said. Links are tight, no play at either end.
Thanks for checking. With a jack under the lower control arm, lift the tire with a pry bar and watch the lower ball joint for any vertical play [SB 21-128].
Pried on both sides and saw zero play at the ball joints. I'm about done with checks. Is it time to buy the part?

snippets.title: Overheating at speed from a restricted radiator core
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at speed and on grades. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

snippets.title: Automatic transmission fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: CVT fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.
